record.original_question: Given functions φ, ψ ∈ C[0,1], do there exist functions F(x,y) and G(x,y) in L²((0,1)²) such that [φ(x) − φ(y)]F(x,y) + [ψ(x) − ψ(y)]G(x,y) = 1 almost everywhere on (0,1)²?

evidence.quote: Given φ, ψ∈C[0,1]. Do there exist F(x,y), G(x,y)∈L²((0,1)²) such that [φ(x)−φ(y)]F + [ψ(x)−ψ(y)]G = 1 a.e. in (0,1)²?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\varphi, \psi \in C[0,1]$ be arbitrary continuous real-valued functions on $[0,1]$. Determine whether there always exist functions $F, G \in L^2((0,1)^2)$ such that
$$[\varphi(x) - \varphi(y)]\, F(x,y) + [\psi(x) - \psi(y)]\, G(x,y) = 1$$
for almost every $(x,y) \in (0,1)^2$. Equivalently: characterize those pairs $(\varphi, \psi)$ of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ for which such an $L^2$-decomposition of the constant function $1$ on the unit square exists.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return direct evidence of a resolution of this specific functional-equation problem (representing the constant 1 on the unit square as a combination of divided-difference factors of two continuous functions with L² coefficients). The problem appears to be a classical open question whose current status could not be confirmed from available sources.

status_evidence.title: Measurable solutions of an alternative functional equation
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work studies related alternative functional equations involving differences φ(x)−φ(y), without resolving the L² decomposition question.
status_evidence.claim: No direct resolution of the stated L²((0,1)²) representation problem was located.
